hints: Focus on what makes an empirical formula different from a molecular formula, think simplest whole number ratio.
Check each formula to see if all the subscripts share a common factor greater than 1 that could be divided out.
Keep the one formula where the atoms are already in their lowest possible ratio, as that cannot be simplified any further.
walkthrough:
**Recall what empirical means**

Think of empirical as the simplest recipe. It shows atoms in the lowest whole number ratio possible.

Rule:
$$\text{empirical formula = molecular formula divided to simplest ratio}$$

**Test each formula for simplification**

Look for a common divisor. For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$, all numbers divide by 2 to give $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$. For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$, all divide by 6 to give $\text{CH}_2$. For $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, both divide by 2 to give $\text{HO}$.

**Spot the one already simplest**

For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$, the ratio 2:4:1 has no common factor greater than 1. It cannot be reduced, so it is already an empirical formula.

options.A: Correct. In C2H4O the ratio C:H:O = 2:4:1 has no common divisor greater than 1, so it is already in its simplest whole number form and can be an empirical formula.
options.B: Incorrect. C2H4O2 can be divided by 2 to give CH2O, so it is a molecular formula (ethanoic acid), not an empirical formula. The trap is missing the common factor of 2.
options.C: Incorrect. C6H12 can be divided by 6 to give CH2, so it is a molecular formula (such as cyclohexane or hexene), not an empirical formula.
options.D: Incorrect. H2O2 can be divided by 2 to give HO, so it is a molecular formula (hydrogen peroxide), not an empirical formula. The trap is confusing a familiar molecular formula with the simplest ratio.
